    • Meta will complete “a full consultation” with news industry leaders before implementing its controversial new terms — even if it means another delay, an executive for the social media organization announced today.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Meta will complete “a full consultation” with news industry leaders before implementing its controversial new terms — even if it means another delay, an executive for the social media organization announced today.

    Sources indicate that “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms patch. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms. Until then our existing terms remain in place.”.

    Meta did not answer Nieman Lab’s questions about which news industry groups and leaders Meta prepares to consult.

    Industry observers note that the proposed terms have drawn criticism because they would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and potentially allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models, with no option to opt out. Last week, Meta revealed it would push back implementation of its fresh terms to November 20 in order to “explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab. Meta had previously revised its new terms to remove the word “train.” No version of the terms has included language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

    Shortly after Stone’s announcement, a Norwegian court blocked Meta’s terms from taking effect on November 20 until the court had assessed their legality, the country’s public broadcaster NRK reported.

    “We are satisfied that the court has agreed with us that Meta holds a dominant position in the relevant market and that the latest terms are unreasonable,” said Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, MBL’s board chair, in a news release. “We are also pleased that the court recognizes that the alternative is that media companies risk losing control over editorial content built up over many years.”.

    In a recent development, since Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15, publishers and politicians around the world have pushed back, filing complaints with national competition authorities, calling on the European Commission to investigate, and writing letters to Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Two United States senators — California Democrat Adam Schiff and Tennessee Republican Marsha Blackburn — each separately wrote to Zuckerberg, insisting that the company withdraw the terms as they’re currently written.

    “After I raised serious concerns about Meta’s aims to scrape and abuse creators’ content, I am pleased the organization is finally acknowledging the concerns of publishers and content creators,” Blackburn said in a statement to Nieman Lab on Wednesday. “While this is a step in the right direction, a vague promise to consult with industry stakeholders and potentially delay implementation is not nearly enough. Meta must commit to meaningful changes that protect the intellectual property rights of American creators, and I will continue holding the company accountable until it does.”.

    According to recent reports, on October 21, the European Publishers Council signed onto a joint letter to the European Commission, asking the Commission to block the terms from taking effect. The letter claims that Meta’s terms violate the Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region.

    EPC executive director Angela Mills Wade said on Wednesday that the organization has not heard from Meta about its letter or its concerns.

    “We welcome Meta’s offer to consult publishers fully, and to delay implementation if necessary,” Mills Wade remarked in an email to Nieman Lab. “However, that consultation must lead to binding contractual safeguards…Using Meta’s services to reach audiences or advertise should not mean granting wider rights to exploit publishers’ journalism, whether collected from websites or uploaded to its platforms. Publishers must retain control over additional uses of their content, including for AI, and the ability to negotiate licenses and payment.”.

    This story has been updated to include a statement from Marsha Blackburn.

    The Latest York Times is adding more AI features to its Cooking app, and users aren’t thrilled

    📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1139 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • In a recent development, we will never sell your address.
    • Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to .
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    In a recent development, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Industry observers note that sometimes, adding just one latest ingredient to a stew can ruin the whole thing.11Olives, yecch. And that’s how at least some New York Times readers see its addition of AI features to its popular Cooking app.

    Here’s Genevieve Ko, NYT Cooking senior editor and columnist, explaining the fresh features:.

    I naïvely assumed A.I. wouldn’t affect my work as a recipe developer and my role at NYT Cooking, where I oversee the editorial side of our recipes and related stories. But as artificial intelligence improved, our product and engineering colleagues saw its potential to help us create features Cooking consumers wanted.

    In a recent development, the Times had previously rolled out AI features aimed at converting volume-based and weight-based measurements (“What’s one cup of bok choy in grams?”) and scaling a recipe up or down to serve more or fewer people. The main new feature is focused on ingredient substitutions.

    According to recent reports, say you’re cooking braised white beans and greens with parmesan, NYT Cooking app in hand. But you notice that you’re out of chard and only have spinach. Cooking veterans know that chard is a rough-and-tumble green that has some backbone22There’s a reason one type of chard is known as “perpetual spinach.”, while spinach is a comparative wimp that will wilt the moment you look at it funny. If you need to sub in spinach for chard, how would the recipe change? Would you, for instance, add the spinach later than you would the chard to account for its pathetic stamina? That’s the sort of thing the new AI feature could account for.

    According to recent reports, cooking staffers “spent countless hours evaluating sample after sample to get the chatbot answers to closely align with how we would answer as culinary experts,” Ko writes. “We applied the same rigor as we do to editing, grounded in Times standards.”.

    But because Ko knows that any AI-powered features are likely to be controversial with a Times audience, she spends quite a lot of space addressing potential objections, everything from “the impact of data centers” to “the concentration of power among A.I. companies” and “the risk of A.I. escaping our control.” These features are designed to enable “the tactile physical pleasure of cooking” and getting a “very real, very human creation” on your table.

    Broadly speaking, commenters weren’t buying it.

    Industry observers note that “What a massive disappointment,” wrote Susan from Fresh Jersey. “The internet is full of AI cooking content. I pay you because I prefer mine done by people.”.

    “This decision misses the mark by such a wide margin it’s baffling,” says Ian from Los Angeles. “And the disclosure just as baffling. It would not be inaccurate to summarize the piece as saying ‘I know doing this is bad and I don’t want to be associated with the bad thing so that’s why we are doing the bad thing.'”.

    Recent findings suggest that “Nobody wants this, it’s bad for cooking, it’s bad for the NYT,” writes Bill from Pittsburgh. “Wasting a column trying to gaslight yourself and your audience into believing that it’s anything but is an embarrassment and a waste of everyone’s time.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE DO NOT DO THIS,” says Judah Mann of Upcoming York. “Oh, wait, you already did. Ok, I’m out.”.

    Or as Naomi from California puts it: “I am sad that AI has breached the one online resource I truly love.”.

    Because I enjoy the irony, I scraped the 171 comments left on the Times’ announcement and asked Codex (running GPT-6.1 Sol, at medium thinking) to do some sentiment analysis. (Twelve of the 171 were comments left by Times staffers; I’m excluding them here.) Roughly 77% of the reader comments were negative about the new AI features, it found, versus 14% positive and the remainder neutral or mixed. Among the biggest categories of complaint: This shouldn’t require AI. AI is destroying the environment. AI is not why I’m paying the Times $390 a year. The adjustments the AI produces are going to be bad.

    Industry observers note that dozens of commenters asked for a way to turn off the feature. “No, not at this time,” Ko responded, “though this feature is completely optional to use.” Indeed: Don’t ask AI to substitute your chard and AI won’t substitute your chard.

    One consistent thread was that cooking is supposed to present you with difficulties and challenges and the whole point is figuring them out by yourself. “Anyone using AI for cooking has no sense of taste and no desire to work out the intricacies of cooking and baking,” writes Michael King from Brooklyn. “To use AI for recipes is beyond the pale. If you are going to use AI, then just cut to the chase and defenestrate yourself.” Or BJ from North Carolina: “So, you’re telling me that I’m too stupid to figure it out on my own?”.

    Meanwhile, the few positive comments tended to focus on how the AI feature had, in fact, made dietary substitutions easier for them. “I love the new AI feature because it rapidly (and so far) accurately converts recipes to gluten free,” Anne Wagner from Kansas City writes. “I don’t cook for stress relief,” says Andy from San Francisco. “I cook to put dinner on the table. Anything that makes the process a little faster or smoother is welcome.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that cloudLinux is the maker of Imunify360 — a suite of security products protecting millions of websites across the web hosting industry — and of CloudLinux OS, the operating system behind a large share of the world's shared hosting. To learn more about our company and products, visit our websites: cloudlinux.com and imunify360.com. Alongside those established product lines we run a small innovation team whose job is to find and prove the next ones.

    According to recent reports, we are looking for a Product Owner to lead that team: a small, senior, fully remote squad of engineers that takes new product concepts from idea to a working MVP in customers' hands, then hands proven products to a product line and moves on to the next concept. You will be accountable for the pipeline of ideas, the speed and rigour with which they are tested, and the evidence behind every go / no-go recommendation.

    This is a hands-on lead role, not pure people management: roughly 50% discovery and leadership (customer conversations, scoping, prioritisation, coaching, reporting to the CPO) and 50% building (prototypes, spikes, design and code review, demo stands). You will not be the team's only builder, but you must be able to build a credible prototype yourself and hold a technical opinion about every part of it.

    In a recent development, you don't need to arrive as an expert in web hosting or security. If you have taken a product from nothing to its first paying customers before — as a founder, an early engineer, or the lead of an incubation team — and you get deep into unfamiliar technical territory fast, we will teach you the market.

    The innovation team sits across CloudLinux and Imunify and owns the product concepts that do not yet have a home in an established product line. Ideas come from customer conversations, industry events, telemetry across more than 80,000 servers and the CPO’s strategy; the team’s job is to turn them into something a customer will pay for within a quarter, using AI coding agents throughout.

    Prototyping and technical direction.

    It has been revealed that we evaluate engineers partly on how effectively they work with coding agents, and in the innovation team this is the main lever on speed. As the lead you model and coach it: prompt specificity, review quality on agent-generated code, context provision, iteration and error recovery, and end-to-end task completion. Expect to use agents to build prototypes, generate test corpora and draft customer-facing material.

    About six in 10 Americans stated they have at least “some” confidence that news organizations will report the upcoming midterm election results accurately, according to a new national survey. But only 32% said they had “quite a bit” or “a great deal” of confidence that journalists would do the job.

    In the survey from Medill Local News Initiative and the Alliance for Trust in Media, 37% said they had either “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” that news outlets would accurately report the election results.

    Recent findings suggest that the survey was completed by a nationally representative sample of 1,057 U.S. adults either online or by telephone earlier this month. The findings echo other national surveys, including a Gallup survey that showed trust in media to report “fully, accurately, and fairly” at 33% — an increase from an all-time low last year.

    According to recent reports, the Medill/Alliance survey found about half of Americans mentioned they had “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” in news outlets to investigate voter fraud claims thoroughly. U.S. President Donald Trump has cast doubt on elections on 70% of days since returning to office — starting with false claims about voter fraud on the first day of his second term.

    In another bleak result from the same poll, slightly more survey respondents remarked journalists manipulate the news for political or commercial purposes than report it accurately. Across the survey, Democrats reported being more confident in (and trusting of) news organizations than Republicans. Nearly 80% of Republicans said journalists try to manipulate the news compared to 38% of independents and 24% of Democrats.

    More on the survey, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, here.

    #31980. Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

    📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4384 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4384 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read

    • Industry observers note that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Recent findings suggest that we will never sell your address.
    • It has been revealed that we have sent a confirmation link to .
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Recent findings suggest that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    It has been revealed that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try newly introduced things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.

    Most local newsrooms in the U.S. have one thing in common: They need more money, and many dream of dollars they can use however they want.

    According to recent reports, RELATED ARTICLEPress Forward awards $20 million to 205 small local newsroomsSophie CulpepperOctober 16, 2024In 2024, Press Forward, the nonprofit trying to mobilize a philanthropic army for local news, declared it would give at least 100 small local newsrooms — those with annual budgets under $1 million — just that type of unrestricted funding. Almost 1,000 newsrooms applied. Ultimately, Press Forward distributed $20 million to 205 outlets. Most of them received $100,000 each, split over two years.

    Recent findings suggest that I wondered what the recipients had done with the money, and which problems it had (or hadn’t) solved. Between May and October, I spoke or emailed with more than 30 grantees.

    According to recent reports, the grantees represented every U.S. state, came from cities, suburbs, and rural areas, and published in multiple languages. They included for-profits and nonprofits, print and digital-only publications, college newsrooms, and public radio stations. Statewide newsrooms with fully staffed teams like The Maine Monitor, scrappy news startups like 285 South, and community newspapers powered by freelancers and part-time staff like the Copper River Record in Alaska all received funding.

    For many newsrooms, Press Forward was the first grant they’d ever applied for. “Many of the country’s newsrooms are small, and few get foundation grants,” noted Press Forward executive director Dale Anglin. The open call was designed to change that and to distribute the money quickly. Grantees were required to complete two LION sustainability audits a year apart; Press Forward is analyzing that data now and will release its findings next month.1.

    According to recent reports, RELATED ARTICLEA study of nonprofit newsrooms reveals some cracks in the model’s foundationSeth C. LewisOctober 6, 2026“People tell me that what Press Forward did was unusual and rare within philanthropy,” said María José Ramírez Braiz, founder and CEO of Midwest-based grantee Te Lo Cuento News.

    “They noted to us at the beginning of the grant period, before the shit hit the fan with the federal government, ‘If you need this money to keep the lights on, keep the lights on,'” said Copper River Record editor Allison Sayer, one of the paper’s two part-time staffers. “I feel that this was really a gift.”.

    Recent findings suggest that first-time grant applicants and recipients, in particular, mentioned Press Forward’s recognition gave them credibility and visibility with other funders. And publishers described the funding as a morale boost that validated low-paid work.

    Sources indicate that “It has been a life-changer, a lifesaver for us,” said Gretchen Sporleder Orr, who publishes the World Journal in southern Colorado with her husband. Her voice broke when she talked to me about the funding. “I don’t know if we would be in business right now if it wasn’t for the Press Forward money.”.

    According to recent reports, the Real WV “would not still exist without Press Forward,” remarked Stephen Baldwin, the site’s volunteer publisher. (He’s also the former minority leader for the West Virginia Senate and a pastor of two churches.) The outlet was one of eight grantees that received just two $25,000 grants over two years. “There’s not exactly a lot of capital floating around West Virginia for nonprofit news,” Baldwin said, “and without this outside impact, we wouldn’t be able to do this work.” But he hopes that the site can be less reliant on grants in the future.

    In a recent development, the funding did not save every recipient. One grantee, Atlanta Civic Circle, shut down earlier this year. Atlanta Civic Circle did not receive its second $50,000 grant because it didn’t complete the first LION audit, Anglin said. (Atlanta Civic Circle did not respond to my request for an interview, but executive director Saba Long wrote on LinkedIn in June that “the funding environment for local nonprofit journalism is extraordinarily difficult right now.”) Other recipients have merged or transformed since applying for the grant.2.

    RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026Medill’s annual State of Local News report, released this month, describes a local news ecosystem in a “state of precarity.” That state of precariousness helps explain how $100,000 over two years can be a “godsend,” a “miracle,” and not enough. As one grantee put it, “Right now, these are shanties built on a beach, waiting for a hurricane to come through.”.

    “Press Forward reached newsrooms that don’t have existing relationships with major national funders,” said Nina Ignaczak, the founder, publisher, and editor of Planet Detroit. “The challenge now is whether the commitment holds.”.

    The funding helped newsrooms keep the lights on, whether they used it to pay bills, pay down debt, make payroll, or as a buffer when something went wrong.

    Recent findings suggest that “The flexibility that Press Forward has given us has allowed us to fill — I wouldn’t say emergencies, but unexpected gaps,” said Richard Young, founder and executive director of CivicLex in Kentucky. It brought on a consulting editor to keep city hall coverage going after losing a reporter, and purchased newly introduced software. Without the funding, CivicLex likely would have had to dip into its reserves, he said.

    Bob Bonnar, publisher of the News Letter Journal in Wyoming, used the first payment from Press Forward to upgrade computers and cameras and give some staffers raises. “That chewed up the money very quickly,” he said, “and I probably should have held some of it back because the News Letter Journal ended up having a pretty rough year in 2025.” He had to use about half of the second $50,000 payment to repay an operating loan. The rest covered the remaining revenue shortfall and kept the organization in the black through the winter.

    Vandana Kumar, publisher of the California-based ethnic media outlet India Currents, described the funding as a “stabilizing force” that allowed the newsroom to keep operating despite a contraction in philanthropic giving and cuts to local government advertising.

    Recent findings suggest that the Copper River Record built infrastructure to host digital ads and created a new website. It held listening sessions with Native villages in its coverage area and donated subscriptions to local Tribal offices. It improved the design of its print newspaper. Sayer paid freelancers to complete Press Pass training and pursued other professional development. And she was able to take on more ambitious stories about PFAS and “forever chemicals.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the Press Forward funding was “the biggest single windfall in nearly 20 years for our small community newspaper,” Sandpoint Reader publisher Ben Olson told me. The Idaho-based paper used the money to travel to the state capital for Press Club awards and design a new media kit, which Olson stated has improved ad sales. The Reader also paid a large chunk of its printing bill, paid its rent a year in advance, and gave staffers bonuses. (The bonuses helped the paper become 100% employee-owned; Olson’s two employees bought in when Olson’s business partner and co-owner retired.).

    The open-ended nature of the grants gave Colorado’s World Journal “the flexibility to be able to make a change, do a thing, and then pivot as needed,” Sporleder Orr mentioned. “When we were in the toilet, all I could think about was, like, ‘Is there going to be anything in the post office today so that I can make payroll?’ ‘Oh, my God, we’ve got to pay rent.’” Sometimes she and her husband skipped their own paychecks to pay staff. The grant gave them “emotional bandwidth” to blueprint ahead.

    Recent findings suggest that many grantees used the funding to hire full- or part-time staffers. Sometimes, that worked out well.

    Recent findings suggest that the Mānoa Mirror, an online newsroom based at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, received two $25,000 grants, which it used to hire a managing editor, a student editorial coordinator, three student reporters, and a social media producer. (The managing editor was paid a stipend, and the other positions were part-time.) The work had previously depended on “faculty goodwill and volunteerism, which was not sustainable for long,” remarked Hye-ryeon Lee, who was professor and chair of the school of communication and information until retiring this summer. With the fresh hires, the site went from publishing a few stories a month to publishing daily.

    According to recent reports, the Real WV’s first LION audit pointed to a need its small team had already recognized: hiring someone to sell ads. It hired a public school teacher with sales experience (including selling ads for the yearbook) part-time.

    The funding allowed Te Lo Cuento News to pay contributors consistently and to add contract, part-time positions including a sales manager, an office administrator, and a couple of reporters. The only position it could sustain beyond the grant period is the part-time sales manager, Ramírez Braiz said.

    In a recent development, the Texas Spur is one of five weekly newspapers owned by Paragraph Ranch Media. Originally, the team planned to use the Press Forward grant to secure a loan to improve firm housing and hire a journalist based in Spur (population 863 as of 2020). But nobody took the newspaper up on the free housing offer, remarked editor and general manager Barbara Brannon. So the company hired four early-career journalists (two full-time, two part-time) living in its 10-county coverage area. Three of the four left for jobs in other industries halfway through their second year. The one who stayed is doing well as a regional sports reporter, Brannon said, and a hire who replaced a person who left is now managing editor for The Post Dispatch.3.

    The turnover Brannon experienced isn’t unique to Spur. Other newsrooms also found hiring with grant money challenging.

    Industry observers note that sometimes, that was because of location. “Had we been able to find the right people from the outset, I believe the grant would have had a greater impact on the business,” remarked Anton Kaufer, regional publisher for Hagadone Media Montana. In rural Northwest Montana, though, recruiting and retaining staff is a challenge, and Hagadone’s Mineral Independent struggled to replace its salesperson and office manager after they retired. The experience “reinforced for us that sustainability isn’t just about having the funding,” Kaufer said. “It’s also about having the people in place to make the most of it.”.

    It has been revealed that the World Journal tried placing an ad for a salesperson with the Colorado Press Association and got “absolutely no interest,” Sporleder Orr noted. “People living in northern Colorado don’t particularly want to come live in a teeny-tiny town in a rural, broke part of the state.” (She credited the grant with giving her the mental space to fire a salesperson who wasn’t working out, then regroup.).

    Other times, the money just wasn’t enough. “The reality is that $100,000 over two years isn’t a lot,” one grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. “You can’t hire somebody with that.”.

    EcoRI’s experience illustrates those limitations. Before receiving the Press Forward grant, EcoRI had used other grant funding and reserves to hire a director of development in a one-year contract position. In its grant application to Press Forward, the team proposed converting that role into a full-time staff position with benefits.

    The salary limited the hiring pool, though. The development director position paid $65,000 a year, which “is really not the market rate for a director of development” in the area, publisher and cofounder Jo Detz mentioned. (She said it should be more like $90,000.) The staffer they ended up hiring came from another state and hadn’t worked in news before. In a staff position, he cost more than he was bringing in. Detz laid him off and eliminated the position last December. She called the experience “heartbreaking.”.

    “At the point where I knew this wasn’t working,” she noted, “there wasn’t enough runway to pivot, rethink, rehire.”.

    Beyond the salary limitations, Detz thinks the development director didn’t have enough runway to succeed. The kind of development the staffer was hired to oversee — major gifts and individual giving — is a long game; “that position would need at least two or three years to begin to see some benefits,” she said. Now, she’s back where she started, juggling fundraising with her other work.

    “I know it’s crazy to say that $100,000 over two years wasn’t enough,” she said, “but it was not enough to make a meaningful difference to our revenue strategy.”.

    Sources indicate that planet Detroit’s Ignaczak was in a unique position: Around the same time the newsroom received the Press Forward grant, Planet Detroit also received a $500,000 three-year grant from the MacArthur Foundation. That grant allowed her to hire a managing editor, she said.

    According to recent reports, ignaczak believes general operating support is what small nonprofit newsrooms need. But to be effective, “I really think fully funding a revenue role for a minimum of three years is what needs to happen to build sustainability, if that is the goal,” she said. “And $100,000 over two years is not enough to achieve that.”.

    Recent findings suggest that notiVisión Georgia, a Spanish-language local news outlet with one full-time staffer, is committed to print in a world moving away from it. The print newspaper is the only way the outlet has been able to use to “generate real economic value,” remarked CEO Mónica Pirela, because it’s where local companies want to place ads. The organization spent some of its Press Forward funds on printing and distribution. Pirela wears “every hat” right now, and the organization’s top need is a dedicated sales manager, she said.

    California’s BenitoLink, meanwhile, used some of the Press Forward funding to begin printing in 2025. That will allow it to apply for newspaper of record status and get paid for running legal notices.

    In a recent development, in Minnesota, Swift County Monitor-News publisher and owner Reed Anfinson called the grant a “godsend” at a time when tariffs and rising gas prices have driven up printing and delivery costs and weakened advertisers’ budgets. The for-profit Monitor-News put some of its Press Forward funding toward redesigning its print newspaper. Anfinson also purchased materials as part of an “Out of Sight/Out of Mind” advertising campaign stressing the value of print. (He created the campaign himself, using Midjourney for the images.) For news organizations in small towns, Anfinson believes, digital revenue will never be enough to sustain operations.

    Some organizations used the funding to expand their remit beyond news.

    Industry observers note that for instance, the Copper River Record partnered with the Copper River Native Association to include weekly language graphics in the paper for Ahtna, a critically endangered language, coordinating with a local kindergarten class. That project required a lot of time and investment up front, Sayer remarked, but it can continue beyond the life of the grant.

    Recent findings suggest that planet Detroit used some Press Forward funding for reporting, but “the most significant thing the grant made possible wasn’t any single story,” Ignaczak mentioned. The grant gave the team time to work on its Civic Action Toolbox, which turns reporting into civic engagement prompts. In a story about a local ballot proposal, for instance, the embedded toolbox flags upcoming public meetings, links to contact information for local representatives, and suggests an organization to follow. The tool is also in beta testing with other newsrooms.

    According to recent reports, “The whole project came from having the space to ask what our readers actually need from us beyond information, and then building toward that,” Ignaczak noted. “Unrestricted funding makes that kind of work possible.”.

    Anfinson of the Monitor-News took the unusual step of writing a grant application on behalf of the local school district, which was losing students to adjacent districts. He used some of the Press Forward funding to match a $2,500 grant to the district. The district then ran $5,000 in ads in a “goodwill effort” to stem declining enrollment. The partnership helped to raise the Monitor-News’s profile, he said, by highlighting the benefits of newspaper advertising.

    Press Forward required grantees to complete two LION sustainability audits. But it also offered optional coaching via the media consulting manufacturer Blue Engine to help implement the first audit’s recommendations. Of the 205 grantees, 154 participated in coaching, Anglin said.

    Industry observers note that the coaching kicked off in January, with most individual coaches and grantees meeting monthly. Multiple participants said the support would have been more beneficial if it were introduced earlier. This was a tradeoff of Press Forward moving rapidly to get money out the door, Anglin said.4.

    Industry observers note that this was the first large, unrestricted grant Austin Common had ever received, and it struggled with how to spend the money. “It felt like a lot of pressure,” said Amy Stansbury, the site’s editor-in-chief and only full-time staffer.

    In a recent development, stansbury wanted to bring on the organization’s first full-time employees, but didn’t want to make those hires (and spend all the grant money) until she had a clear blueprint. The coaching helped her figure out which hires made the most strategic sense and how to budget for them.

    According to recent reports, A few publishers were lukewarm about the substance of the coaching, but the majority I heard from were enthusiastic. At first, Baldwin was skeptical and worried the coaching might amount to “checking a box.” In practice, though, he said it’s been “tremendously helpful” for tasks like writing the job description for the Real WV’s sales position.

    In a recent development, sporleder Orr called the coaching “incredible.” The monthly sessions helped her with everything from tackling grant proposals to improving her Google Analytics skills. The combination of money and coaching, she added, “makes sure that the recipients don’t just continue doing business as usual.”.

    In addition to the funding, Press Forward paid for grantees to attend conferences. Anglin said 111 grantees attended the Lenfest News Philanthropy Summit in Philadelphia in 2025, 81 attended the same conference (which I also attended) in 2026, and 87 attended the Business of Local conference in Salt Lake City in 2025. A handful of grantees attended affinity conferences.

    Stansbury found attending conferences for the first time helpful and eye-opening. It taught her “there’s this secret shadow world of [invitation-only] foundation and grant funding.” Press Forward’s travel support to attend a national conference was “transformative” for India Currents, Kumar mentioned, giving it visibility and access to relationship-building.

    To small newsrooms, the grant felt like a Press Forward stamp of approval that put them on the map for other funders. The Mirror’s Lee called the Press Forward funding “instrumental” in securing a $20,000 grant from a local foundation. But that was an exception among publishers I heard from; most didn’t feel the visibility and credibility conferred by the grant directly translated to other funders giving them more money.

    According to recent reports, so several publishers, including Ramírez Braiz of Te Lo Cuento News, would like to see Press Forward go a step further and make individual introductions to funders. “Those more personal introductions can make a major difference for small organizations,” she said.

    Ramírez Braiz also called for “more shared learning around outcomes and impact.” Few grantees had a good sense of what others in the cohort were up to, and some were interested in more knowledge sharing with peer organizations, though the day-to-day grind of keeping one’s own newsroom running was a common impediment.

    According to recent reports, since 2023, Anglin said, Press Forward’s network of more than 130 funders has invested $258 million directly in newsrooms. That suggests that over half of the more than $400 million the coalition claims it’s invested has gone to newsrooms.

    In a recent development, when Press Forward first confirmed the direct funding for newsrooms, it “felt really awesome,” the grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. To the grantee, it was meaningful to see Press Forward give funding to more organizations than planned in response to the scale of need. But when Press Forward went on to a second funding round in which single organizations, including both newsrooms and newsroom-adjacent organizations like the International Women’s Media Foundation and LION, received as much as $1.5 million for infrastructure projects, the same grantee said it felt like “a slap in the face.”.

    “Many of the problems newsrooms face aren’t unique to them individually,” Anglin stated. “If we are attempting to solve problems at scale, we have to intervene not just at the newsroom level, but at the systems level, too.” She said that because many of the infrastructure grantees serve multiple newsrooms, “investing in them creates a multiplier effect across the industry.”.

    Industry observers note that the argument that funding support organizations and infrastructure lifts more boats is “a cop-out,” this publisher said. “I think the philanthropists know it, I think the associations know it, and I think the potential grantees that are not funders or associations or intermediaries know it.”.

    Industry observers note that young had a different perspective. Because of CivicLex’s broad scope, it seeks out funding from both democracy funders and journalism funders. Young thinks local news funders are way ahead on getting dollars into local communities.

    According to recent reports, “I think Press Forward has done one of the more effective jobs of anything I’ve seen in the broader landscape of my world, and the civic renewal space, of delivering resources to the local level,” he remarked. (He added, “No one is ever happy in the local news ecosystem when I say that folks in the local news ecosystem don’t know how good they have it. That does not win me a lot of friends.”).

    Most publishers I heard from see grants like this as critical to continued operation, yet they’re wary of overreliance on philanthropy.

    Young said he’d be surprised if local news is still a focus for national philanthropy in eight years. “Filling your cup up with money that will be impossible to recover in four years is a danger zone,” he added.

    Right now, more than 80% of Planet Detroit’s revenue mix comes from foundations. Ignaczak remarked the organization hopes to bring that down to 50% by 2028. “But for nonprofit newsrooms covering environmental and public health complications in a mid-size metro, general operating grants aren’t a crutch,” she said. “They’re infrastructure.”.

    Recent findings suggest that as for Press Forward, “Time will tell, as these grants go away, what impact [they’ve] actually had on the newsrooms that received [them], how many have managed to build sustainability,” she added. “I think a newsroom that needed $50,000 to survive to next year had problems that $50,000 isn’t going to solve.”.

    Industry observers note that LOOKOUT executive director Jake Hylton believes there’s enough funding to go around. “While there may not be enough to support every single newsroom at a very large amount,” he remarked, “I do believe that there is a larger investment in news that could be done.”.

    It has been revealed that A second grantee who asked to stay anonymous was blunt about their fears for the future. “We’re scared shitless about 2027,” this person said, “because not only is the Press Forward money not returning, we also see none of the national grants that sustained us in 2024 and previous years.”.

    The Copper River Record was in the black before receiving this grant, and the lean paper’s fixed overhead remains low. For the Record, Press Forward has been like “a fairy godmother,” Sayer said.

    It has been revealed that “I’m not going to lie: I will miss having the money to say yes to any reasonable story,” she continued. “But I think that, even going back to our original budget, the strength of what we learned will continue to help us deliver a higher quality paper that is more relevant to the communities we serve.”.

    Sources indicate that the Sandpoint Reader, Olson said, is “surviving” right now. “We’d love to be thriving,” he added, “but we’re happy to continue to survive when many print publications aren’t.” He credited the Press Forward grant with giving the burned-out team “the chance to fall in love with our industry again.”.

    Sporleder Orr feels nervous about what’s ahead, but with the World Journal in a much more comfortable cash flow position, she and her husband are “in a way better mental state about the business.”.

    “We feel good about the future right now, that we are going to be able to keep going and make it,” she noted. “We’re back to, ‘This is what we do ’til we die.'”.

    #31974. Industry News: Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

    📖 Baca

    Industry News: Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

    📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5127 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • In a recent development, we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • Grokipedia demonstrates that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    In a recent development, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Grokipedia demonstrates that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.

    It has been revealed that when I saw Grokipedia’s articles about me, the memories came rushing back: my 19 years in minor league baseball, including that impressive season with the Montgomery Rebels when I hit 20 home runs. I was lean back then — 6 feet tall and 168 pounds — and earned a career batting average just under .300. I became a minor league coach and managed the Chicago White Sox for a short stint in 1970, which Grokipedia mentioned “highlighted [my] readiness for higher-level responsibilities.”.

    I then attended Arizona State University, switched to a career in journalism, created the fact-checking site PolitiFact, won a Pulitzer Prize, and now teach journalism at Duke University.

    Ah, the memories!…except that I never played minor league baseball, never managed the White Sox, and can only dream about being 6 feet tall. (I’m 5’8″.) Grokipedia, the AI-written encyclopedia of Elon Musk, has confused me with Marion Danne “Bill” Adair, who died in 2002.

    Recent findings suggest that that article and another one about “Bill Adair (journalist)” — which really is me — illustrate the many flaws of Grokipedia, which launched a year ago. The articles are littered with mistakes and superfluous details. They are terribly written and ridiculously long. If Grok, the AI engine that wrote this turgid prose, were a student in one of my writing courses, I would give it a D. (Editor’s note: After this article was published, someone updated the inaccurate Grok pages. The original versions are linked here.).

    Sources indicate that still, the articles provide valuable lessons for Wikipedia editors who are debating how and when to use AI. Grokipedia adds fresh content and context that Wikipedia often lacks. It demonstrates that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet and summarizing them in sweeping prose. It can also provide balance to articles that need it.

    Grok can’t write worth a lick, but it demonstrates how Wikipedia can take advantage of AI at a time when overworked editors are trying to keep the encyclopedia alive.

    Musk introduced Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he stated was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet. With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a new version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.” When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had substantial aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video. Maybe someday. For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia demonstrates edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make. Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk. Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors demonstrated Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too swiftly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a big scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s notable and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors highlighted Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok remarked I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too quickly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a massive scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s important and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “Newly introduced pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok reveals that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities.     • You’ll take ownership of customer billing inquiries across EMEA, partnering directly with customers and working cross-functionally with our Billing Engineering team.
    • This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about helping millions of customers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We’re looking for a Billing Support Specialist to play a critical role in shaping our billing experience.

    You’ll take ownership of customer billing inquiries across EMEA, partnering directly with customers and working cross-functionally with our Billing Engineering team. Beyond resolving complications, you’ll help identify patterns, improve workflows, and contribute to product enhancements that scale.

    This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about helping millions of customers.

    Provide initial and timely responses to all support cases for a variety of topics, from billing or pre-sales requests to usage optimization or disputes.

    Debug/Identify user-specific concerns such as failed payments, unsettled invoices, payment extensions.

    Triage support cases including directing customers to previous answers, code examples, documentation, or escalating to specific technical or business team members.

    Identify where internal tooling might be developed or obtained to improve support efficiency.

    Reproduce challenges, create test cases and improve test coverage, if you have experience with testing.

    Experienced in customer support, with 2+ years of experience providing billing support to technical customers.

    Excellent communication skills and fluency in English.

    Communicate clearly across both technical and non-technical audiences.

    Have experience in async or globally distributed teams.

    Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving promptly.

    Being proficient in SQL is a bonus.

    Recent findings suggest that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    According to recent reports, supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are key to us.

    Once a year, the entire firm gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Industry observers note that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    Right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each manufacturer’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft said they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.”.

    Anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI says it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year.

    Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an crucial step,” writing in a tweet that the manufacturer supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

    A few other highlights from the earnings:.

    According to recent reports, let me just start by saying, we’ve got really big ambitions in video for The Times to be as preferred a brand to watch as it is to read and listen. This is a kind of long bet that we can grow engagement from the audience we have, and also grow audience, because we’re going to engage new people in different ways. I’m not sure what you’re referring to operationally. We’ve been in a sort of steady state of scaling production in the newsroom of video, and that’s happening in myriad ways. We’ve got a big and expansive indicates group, and I referred to that in my prepared remarks, where we’re putting a lot of resource and energy into a growing stable of shows that are getting more and more cultural resonance.

    According to recent reports, we also continue to have a substantial effort on visual investigations, which we’ve referred to in prior quarters and in prepared remarks. I referred today in my prepared remarks to a very big effort in the development of short-form video. We’ve talked about that pretty extensively, so a lot of reporter video. Then also now, we’re rolling out more assertively some short-form video franchises, like the one I mentioned from our fashion critic, Vanessa Friedman. We’ve got another one coming from one of the hosts of The Daily. All that, I would just say, reflects a sort of big effort to sort of harness the investment we’ve already made in extraordinary journalists and journalism and put it into newly introduced forms.

    I think you’ve heard both [EVP and CFO Will Bardeen] and I talk about this is a key area of investment, and we expect it to drive more engagement, and ultimately, over time, we expect that to enhance our monetization.

    “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”.

    Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

    But not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

    In a recent development, “Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres stated. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”.

    Recent findings suggest that mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

    Recent findings suggest that to reach new audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres said she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Recent findings suggest that from the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

    Industry observers note that “The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” stated Torres, who is at the moment a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Sources indicate that another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Industry observers note that mongabay now plans its multimedia packages for big investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres said. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”.

    Industry observers note that not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

    “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres stated. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”.

    CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

    In a recent development, “We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he said. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”.

    Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

    Sources indicate that RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler remarked. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”.

    Looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.).

    Today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler mentioned. Only 21% were “doom only.”.

    The video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

    It has been revealed that “We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres said. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”.

    What video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler mentioned.).

    “I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler noted. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”.

    Part of the problem, he said, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”.

Then you lead technical delivery management with our engineers, steering increments, dependencies and decisions until you get it live and prove the value. You won't design and hand over: you stay until it works in production, and keep evolving it.

    It has been revealed that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Industry observers note that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    In a recent development, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    College football already has an Orange Bowl, a Peach Bowl, and a Citrus Bowl, so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl.

    In a recent development, but this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.).

    On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins unveiled the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:.

    The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

    Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

    A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

    But we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM.

    According to recent reports, for those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one organization or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

    This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

    It has been revealed that indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The Newly introduced York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.).

    Collins indicates The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the Upcoming Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently remarked no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.).

    So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The Latest Orleans Bowl.

    I love New Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM.

    Then the folks who run the Latest Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our plans to highlight our mascot:.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM.

    Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in Upcoming Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and mentioned it straight up: "No.".

    Industry observers note that we asked why. They said politics. And the Sickos Guy.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:40 AM.

    While the Newly introduced Orleans Bowl might be out, several presently-brand-free possibilities remain, including the Frisco Bowl in newly blue Texas — the state also home to The Onion’s rival to the death, Alex Jones.
