    #31921. Tech Report: Branded Query Data Is Now In The Google Search Console API via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (732 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Branded Query Data Is Now In The Google Search Console API via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (732 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google has announced that it is adding three features from its Search Console Performance report to the Search Analytics API.
    • According to Google’s blog post announcing this, the API now supports the branded queries filter, multimodal web search data (web multimodal), and filters that are able to track multiple countries or device types within one API call.
    • The blog post explains how all three items have been available in the Performance report since they were first implemented.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google has announced that it is adding three features from its Search Console Performance report to the Search Analytics API. This means website developers and tool makers can build these features directly into their automated reporting systems.

    According to Google’s blog post announcing this, the API now supports the branded queries filter, multimodal web search data (web multimodal), and filters that are able to track multiple countries or device types within one API call.

    The blog post explains how all three items have been available in the Performance report since they were first implemented. The post then describes the API versions as a solution to “stitching together separate requests or maintaining complex keyword regex lists”.

    Industry observers note that your API results can now include a brandedClassification dimension, which enables you to use either the values BRANDED or NON_BRANDED for filtering or grouping based on branded vs. non-branded searches. According to the API reference documentation, this newly introduced dimension provides data only for top-level properties, starting Feb. 21, 2026; however, if a property does not meet the required number of queries and impressions, you will receive an empty table (no rows), the blog post notes.

    The API reference documentation also states that the branded classification dimension field accepts only the equals operator, and you cannot apply filters or groupings with it in requests with a query filter applied.

    Google’s earlier announcement showed the branded and non-branded options in the Performance report:.

    In March, a Search Console user posted a question noting that their branded breakdown only started at approximately Feb. 21. They then asked if it would be possible to have prior data broken out into two different categories. Google’s John Mueller responded that there is “a point when the data starts being tracked,” as reported by Roger Montti.

    Searches with Google Lens provide multimodal performance metrics when type is set to webMultimodal, as do Circle to Search on an Android device and uploading images to Google Search, according to the reference.

    Recent findings suggest that after multimodal reporting was enabled by Search Console on Sept. 24, I reported that the API reference did not have a separate multimodal type value listed. The reference, last updated Nov. 16, now lists one.

    Google’s September announcement illustrated the multimodal option in the report’s search-type filter:.

    Sources indicate that google’s September announcement also listed Chrome’s right-click “Search this image” feature, and the Performance report help page includes Chrome image search. The API post and reference don’t mention Chrome.

    Recent findings suggest that the Nov. 16 post claims multimodal data “will also be available in BigQuery for properties with an active bulk data export” but doesn’t give a date. As of Nov. 16, the bulk export table reference lists six search types, with no multimodal value yet.

    Recent findings suggest that A brand-newly introduced field, filterLists, enables customers to filter results by multiple countries or multiple devices in one request. The examples given in the post are country-based groupings like EMEA, LATAM or DACH.

    The reference limits filterLists to country and device dimensions and matches on exact values only. Consumers cannot use the same dimension (country or device) in filters and in filterLists in the same request.

    In a recent development, on eligible properties, the new feature allows teams using the API to capture a branded/non-branded split in their reporting tools, starting Feb. 21, 2026. For data prior to this date, the API’s split has no ability to break out branded vs. non-branded search traffic.

    Industry observers note that google uses an AI-assisted process to determine which searches are branded or non-branded. According to Google’s November 2025 announcement, “some queries may occasionally be misidentified”. To identify discrepancies, run the API branded/non-branded split alongside a brand regex you have been using and see where they differ.

    In a recent development, as of Nov. 16, the API reference does not indicate if web results include webMultimodal data. Before adding your web and webMultimodal totals together, check how your API web numbers match against the text-based and multimodal numbers in the Performance report.

    In a recent development, as of Nov. 16, neither Google’s post nor the API reference explains how far back webMultimodal data goes. Check the API reference and the bulk export table reference for a BigQuery date, the start date for multimodal history, and any mention of Chrome image search.

But in the Twin Cities, Neal St. Anthony writes, a rich local news ecosystem offers a more hopeful picture. The metro area of more than 3 million people is home to The Minnesota Star Tribune, public radio powerhouse MPR, local TV stations, and multiple successful nonprofit startups, from nearly two-decade-old MinnPost to Sahan Journal (whose founder, Mukhtar Ibrahim, also released The Somali Brief this fall). Axios has published an Axios Local newsletter for the Twin Cities since 2021, and this summer, The New York Times launched its own Twin Cities local newsletter.

    Sources indicate that RELATED ARTICLEWith Washington Post Local diminished, other news sites step up their D.C. coverageSophie CulpepperMarch 5, 2026The question this ecosystem raises, according to St. Anthony, is “whether the Twin Cities represents the potential future of local news in metros across the country: a robust ecosystem with no dominant mass-market player but more news outlets tailored to smaller, niche audiences with narrower but deep interests.” (That description brings to mind other urban media markets where a diffuse ecosystem of smaller, newer players have stepped up as legacy media pulls back.).

    Industry observers note that “There is a healthy degree of vitality in local news in the Twin Cities. The story elsewhere is ‘news deserts’ and little original journalism,” University of Minnesota professor Benjamin Toff told St. Anthony. While local institutions like the Star Tribune have survived, he added, “it’s not immune to industry forces, including the veritable disappearance of print.”.

Patrick Reinhart, VP of Services and Thought Leadership at Conductor, joined me on the SEJ Podcast to discuss what enterprise brands should be trying to achieve with answer engine optimization.

    Sources indicate that we talk about the difference between citations and recommendations, how AI can repeat outdated information about your business, and why AEO needs input from SEO, PR, social, and leadership.     But he’s creative. Seeing that creativity find a different canvas gave me ideas. There are a lot of ways we can implement this throughout our lives.

    Patrick: The best way is just to do it. I see so many companies and people stuck in analysis paralysis, asking, “What should I do?”.

    In a recent development, something. Just start learning.

    It took me a minute when this started, but I feel pretty good about where I am. I still have eons to learn about using this technology.

    It’s cool that your son has that ability. I’m going to tell my son to do that instead of playing Roblox, which I’m sure he’s doing right now. Half my salary goes to Robux.

    Loren: Where can our listeners and viewers find you online and follow up with questions?

    Patrick: The best place is LinkedIn or Conductor.com. I also do a monthly webinar called 30|30.

    AI Visibility Data: Avoid 4 Traps & Prioritize The Right Work

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1018 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, this post was sponsored by TransPerfect Digital.
    • It has been revealed that your AI visibility dashboard reveals brand mentions, sentiment scores, and frequently cited sources.
    • Which data sources actually help increase AI visibility?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, this post was sponsored by TransPerfect Digital. The opinions expressed in this article are the sponsor’s own.

    It has been revealed that your AI visibility dashboard reveals brand mentions, sentiment scores, and frequently cited sources. But what do they tell you?

    Which data sources actually help increase AI visibility?

    AI tools show 72% visibility; is this good?

    What strategies does AI visibility data inform?

    As you can imagine, the logical next steps are to choose KPIs that reflect your business goals, then use your AI visibility data to identify the next best steps.

    However, the challenge is understanding what to measure, how to analyze, and which online tips are helpful, useless, or harmful.

    These myths and misinterpretations that can steer your generative engine optimization (GEO) work toward the wrong priorities.

    The four traps below will help you interpret those signals before changing your content, channel strategy, or budget.

    Not sure which AI visibility findings deserve your team’s time?

    Join Julie Franck of TransPerfect Digital and Antonia Breitenfellner of Peec AI for AI Search: Turn Insight Into Impact to explore which insights to act on.

    The first trap is treating AI visibility tracking like a keyword-ranking report.

    A score is only useful if the questions being measured reflect the people you want to reach.

    Instead, choose prompts that reflect your customers’ questions across buying stages, markets, and AI platforms before deciding what to change.

    Sources indicate that imagine a tool reports 72% visibility. That number could look reassuring while describing a narrow set of branded, informational questions from one customer group, market, and AI platform.

    If you cannot tell whether that score includes the questions your buyers ask when comparing options, it cannot tell you which content needs attention.

    To assess our example 72% score, check whether it represents the customers and buying decisions that matter to your business, using a consistent set of prompts for comparison.

    That means checking coverage before setting a target or commissioning content. Use the prompt-library checks below to find which audiences, questions, or markets are missing.

    Pro Tip: For help assessing which visibility findings deserve action, join AI Search: Turn Insight Into Impact and bring your score-assessment questions to the Q&A.

    To determine if your AI visibility score is helpful, check its coverage:.

    Pro Tip: Be sure to analyze each individual model, not overall LLM performance, as each retrieves and cites differently.

    Use first-party data to map actual user behavior to your objectives and ICPs, then add questions from sales conversations, customer support, and local teams.

    Adapt the questions to each market’s language and customer needs rather than translating one country’s list.

    Recent findings suggest that list the audiences, products and services, markets, and AI platforms your business needs to monitor. Choose a tool that meets those requirements, and check its visibility definition before comparing scores between tools.

    In a recent development, prompt wording varies and results can be personalized, so one answer is not a stable ranking. Use these checks to identify recurring patterns per topic cluster, category, or product line before assigning work:.

    Recent findings suggest that the second trap is accepting a headline metric without checking what it means for your business. Visibility scores, sentiment labels, and citation counts need context: your positioning, goals, customers, and products.

    Consider an illustrative example: a tool labels a luxury brand negatively because answers describe its products as expensive.

    That description may reinforce premium positioning. But an answer saying the product is poor value, unreliable, or unsuitable for its intended buyer would raise a different issue.

    Industry observers note that before creating a corrective task, connect the metric to your business goal and read the underlying answers. For the sentiment example, ask:.

    Match your response to what the answer actually states:.

    Apply this business-context check to every headline metric, not just sentiment, so you do not miss opportunities or spend time correcting something that supports your strategy.

    The third trap is turning every finding into a to-do or adopting a fashionable GEO tactic without checking its strategic value. A frequently cited source can reveal an information need without dictating a channel.

    Industry observers note that suppose Reddit keeps appearing in answers about your product category. Before adding Reddit activity to your plan, examine the cited discussions.

    A task such as “post on Reddit” names a channel without explaining the customer need. Identifying that need first makes it easier to choose where and how to contribute.

    Industry observers note that prioritize findings that reveal an important customer need and support your business goals; defer those that do not. Apply that test to Reddit:.

    For help thinking through which findings deserve action, bring your questions to the webinar’s Q&A. The discussion will explore what marketers should prioritize, not simply which metrics they can track.

    The fourth trap is treating visibility as the business goal, then assigning it a precise revenue contribution the evidence cannot support.

    A recorded AI referral and an AI-influenced decision are not the same thing. Someone may discover, compare, or shortlist a brand in an AI answer without clicking through to its website.

    Recent findings suggest that low recorded referral traffic does not establish low influence. Equally, rising branded search does not prove AI caused the increase.

    Keep these signals distinct in your reporting:.

    Choose business measures that fit your goal, such as qualified inquiries or sales, and show them alongside visibility signals without claiming a causal connection you have not established.

    Before assigning work, review these four questions:.

    Those checks help you decide what to investigate, what to change, and what to leave alone.

They will discuss meaningful visibility insights, practical priorities, and turning those insights into business action, with time for Q&A.

    #31915. A Trusted Optimizely Script Carried Malware To 178 Organizations via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1035 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    A Trusted Optimizely Script Carried Malware To 178 Organizations via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1035 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that websites running Optimizely Web Experimentation served malicious JavaScript to visitors on Nov.
    • Scott Helme, founder of Report URI, a organization that sells tools for monitoring the scripts that run on websites, reported finding the code in snippets belonging to 178 organizations, including Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce and GitLab.
    • Sources indicate that optimizely’s status page says an unauthorized party “exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation” to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that websites running Optimizely Web Experimentation served malicious JavaScript to visitors on Nov. 16 after an attacker added it to their projects inside Optimizely. The code swapped crypto wallet addresses, looked for payment cards typed into sites’ own forms, and loaded exploit kits aimed at iPhones and iPads running older versions of iOS.

    Scott Helme, founder of Report URI, a organization that sells tools for monitoring the scripts that run on websites, reported finding the code in snippets belonging to 178 organizations, including Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce and GitLab.

    Sources indicate that optimizely’s status page says an unauthorized party “exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation” to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. In a statement to BleepingComputer, the tech giant said the vulnerability was “in the Experimentation account signup flow” and that it has notified all affected customers. Teams running Optimizely Web have checks to make inside their own accounts, starting with every project’s custom code and everyone who can edit it, according to Helme.

    Sources indicate that the way Optimizely Web works is by having each client load a JavaScript snippet hosted on Optimizely’s Content Delivery Network (CDN). In addition to the client-specific experiment data, this snippet can have an optional Project JavaScript section which allows clients to input their own custom JavaScript that will run with every page load.

    According to recent reports, report URI found that the hacker had created malicious code within the Project JavaScript section but left everything else about the script intact; thus, even though the malicious code was present, the script still came from cdn.optimizely.com, a domain that every affected website already trusted. Affected were also scripts that clients served from their own domains, as well as those for optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com.

    Optimizely’s statement to BleepingComputer claims the company has “blocked access to the vulnerable path and deployed a fix” and has “ended active sessions, revoked tokens, and reset access for affected user accounts.”.

    Helme found that the inserted code would load a second script which would replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses with the attacker’s. Starting at 1:43 p.m. UTC, it would watch the website’s own form fields for credit card information, expiration date and CVV, and attempt to submit this information to the attacker after receiving all three. Credit card information entered via hosted payment iframes (such as Stripe and Adyen) was outside the script’s reach.

    It has been revealed that helme’s team reviewed a total of 1,611 Optimizely snippet files, most of which came from Report URI’s own crawl data; 188 contained malicious code. Helme believes the actual number is likely greater than 188. Report URI first saw the code in a snippet on Nov. 16 at 4:21 a.m. UTC, and all of the infected files were clean as of 11:11 p.m. UTC the same day.

    The Content Security Policy (CSP), as a header, tells the browser the scripts that a website can use (the script-src section) and to which locations it may transmit data (the connect-src section). Report URI then compared those policies for the affected organizations’ sites against those required by the malicious code. Out of the total of 159 organizations that were reviewed, 68 had no Content Security Policy at all and 50 did have a Content Security Policy that permitted both the malicious code and transmission of sensitive user information.

    According to recent reports, seventeen organizations permitted the malicious code to execute, but prevented it from transmitting the user’s information due to restrictions placed upon their connect-src directives. However, this did not prevent the malicious actor from substituting the intended recipient’s wallet address with the attacker’s. Additionally, 24 of the organizations, or 15%, completely blocked execution of the malicious code, and they differed from the other organizations studied in having a restrictive script-src directive.

    It has been revealed that helme wrote that listing Optimizely’s domain name within an organization’s Content Security Policy does not provide protection because the malicious code originated from that same domain. A common Content Security Policy setting, 'strict-dynamic', permits access to be granted to the malicious code if it is inserted into the content via the Optimizely snippet. Likewise, an 'unsafe-eval' setting allows an inline version of the malicious code to be executed when access to the original version has been denied.

    It has been revealed that optimizely’s Content Security Policy help page lists 'strict-dynamic' in the recommended script-src line. Certain Optimizely features such as audiences with custom JavaScript conditions are unavailable unless 'unsafe-eval' is used, and the page’s full sample Content Security Policy includes 'unsafe-eval'.

    It has been revealed that helme says the Project JavaScript in all of the Optimizely Web customer projects and the custom JavaScript in their experiments should be opened to find 1688360.cc, atob( and any other scripts that were written by someone other than the development team. You also need to review who has write access among your users, API tokens and integrations and then rotate your credentials.

    The change history page from Optimizely indicates that each project’s History logs every Project JavaScript change and that you can filter the log entries based upon how they were made (via the REST API or via the Web Experimentation interface). There are no steps listed for customers on the status page.

    Optimizely’s documentation example below shows the History navigation item and the Type, Date and Source filters.

    According to recent reports, project JavaScript is run on every page that loads an Optimizely snippet, so this attack was able to hit visitors without changing anything on the affected sites’ own code. The change sat in customers’ Optimizely projects, which put your Optimizely account (which includes who can edit Project JavaScript and what API tokens exist) on the same audit list as your site.

    Optimizely told BleepingComputer it’s continuing to investigate and will publish updates on its status page, which listed the incident as Monitoring on the morning of Nov. 17. Its status page, X post and statement don’t say how many customer projects were affected or how a flaw in the signup flow let the attacker change existing customer projects. Until they do, the checks inside the account are the ones teams can run themselves.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that liveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

    The Staff GTM Systems Engineer at LiveKit is the technical owner and architect of the systems that power our go-to-market engine. You'll decide how our GTM stack is designed, what we build versus buy, and where we invest next — and you'll be hands-on building it: Salesforce architecture, integrations, enrichment pipelines, and the agentic workflows that help Sales and Marketing move faster and smarter.

    Sources indicate that salesforce is our system of record for revenue, pipeline, and customer data. HubSpot is our marketing layer for campaigns and lead generation, and what it captures needs to flow cleanly and reliably into Salesforce. Around them sits a growing stack of enrichment, sales intelligence, billing, and data platform tools. You'll own the architecture that ties it all together: disciplined change management, observable pipelines, data models built for AI consumption, and agentic workflows that act on GTM signals at scale — designed to serve the business for years, not quarters.

    In a recent development, this role sits at the intersection of GTM, Data, Finance, and Engineering. You'll work directly with senior leaders to shape the GTM systems roadmap, turn business strategy into technical looks, and guide decisions that span multiple teams. You'll also help grow the engineers around you, setting the technical standards and practices the team builds on.

    It has been revealed that you understand the difference between owning a system and gatekeeping one. Sales lives in Salesforce. Marketing lives in HubSpot. Your job is to make sure both are governed well enough that others can work in them effectively, and powerful enough that the GTM team can do things they couldn't do before.

    You'll thrive as a Staff GTM Systems Engineer if you:.

    Are known as the go-to person for tough technical problems, and have good judgment about which ones matter most.

    Think in systems and long time horizons, and can make confident architectural decisions with incomplete information.

    Can clearly explain complex technical concepts and tradeoffs to engineers and executives alike.

    Believe systems should be managed with engineering discipline.

    Ship fast and reliably — your work holds up in production.

    Are a fast learner, frequently picking up newly introduced languages and tools.

    Find real satisfaction in mentoring other engineers and helping them grow.

    Own the architecture of the GTM systems stack: define how Salesforce, HubSpot, enrichment, sales intelligence, billing, and the data platform fit together, and write the technical strategy that guides how it evolves.

    Lead build-vs-buy and procurement decisions: evaluate vendors, run proofs of concept, assess security and integration fit, and partner with Director of GTM Systems and Analytics, Finance, Legal, and IT on selection and renewals.

    Shape the GTM systems roadmap with senior leaders across Sales, Marketing, RevOps, Finance, and Engineering: align on requirements, sequence investments, make clear tradeoffs, and lead cross-functional initiatives to completion.

    Own Salesforce as the engineering system of record for revenue: data model, flows and automation, validation rules, field governance, and access control.

    Own HubSpot for campaigns and lead generation, along with the HubSpot-Salesforce sync — so leads, contacts, and engagement signals reach the revenue pipeline without drift or silent failures.

    Build and maintain integrations across the GTM stack, and partner with GTM Analytics Engineering on reliable data flows to the central data platform.

    Design and deploy agentic workflows that consume GTM data, surface actionable signals, and automate manual operations — and set the patterns and guardrails others build on.

    Establish observability and change management for critical GTM systems: alerts, dashboards, and runbooks; reviewed code changes, documented config, and rollback paths.

    Mentor engineers across experience levels and set the technical standards for the team.

    Partner with the Billing Systems Engineer to automate the CPQ-to-Billing handoff.

    Extensive engineering experience in GTM or business systems, including owning a GTM stack's architecture end to end — build-vs-buy calls, vendor evaluations, and systems designed for a multi-year horizon.

    According to recent reports, deep, hands-on Salesforce expertise — you understand the data model, have built complex flows and automation, and you think about it as an engineering system, not an admin tool. This is the primary bar.

    HubSpot experience in a marketing context, including the HubSpot-Salesforce sync and what breaks and why.

    Technical depth beyond the UI — you've built integrations with APIs, webhooks, and event streams, and you know when a native tool (a Flow, a Clay table, a HubSpot workflow) is the right answer versus when it's time to write code.

    Agentic workflow experience — you've designed and deployed AI agents that act on GTM data in production.

    Strong change management practices — you've shipped changes to live systems while protecting active deals and campaigns.

    Experience influencing senior stakeholders — translating business strategy into system requirements and roadmaps.

    A history of mentoring engineers, from early-career to senior.

    Salesforce CPQ: approvals, order forms, discounting rules, and the closed-won-to-billing path.

    SQL and data modeling fluency; familiarity with a warehouse-centric stack (BigQuery, Snowflake, dbt, reverse ETL).

    Experience with billing platforms (Stripe, Zuora, Maxio) and the handoffs between GTM systems and billing.

    Experience managing a GTM tooling budget or vendor portfolio.

    Experience as a technical lead on a GTM or business systems team.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Contribute to open source alongside world-class engineers.

    Competitive salary and equity package.

    Health, dental, and vision benefits.

    #31912. Date: Confirmed, Rating: Meets Expectations, Comments: None via @sejournal, @pedrodias

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2026 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Date: Confirmed, Rating: Meets Expectations, Comments: None via @sejournal, @pedrodias

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2026 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the routine is familiar by now.
    • Recent findings suggest that I’ve watched this for most of 20 years.
    • Industry observers note that when Google launched what the industry later called Panda, in February 2011, they wrote a post about it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that the routine is familiar by now. Google posts a sentence. It has a name, a start time, and a note that the rollout may take up to two weeks. Within the hour, somebody has published a “what we know so far.” By the evening, there’s a list of winners and losers. Before the week is out, with the rollout still running, there’s a recovery guide in seven steps.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ve watched this for most of 20 years. The only part that has changed is the sentence. It used to be longer.

    Industry observers note that when Google launched what the industry later called Panda, in February 2011, they wrote a post about it. The post said what the change was for: sites that add little, copy from others, or just aren’t very useful. It said how major it was: 11.8% of queries. You could argue with the result, and plenty did, but there was a stated target to argue with.

    Here is the entry for the November 2026 core patch, which started on Nov. 10. It was released. It applies globally and in all languages. It may take up to two weeks. That’s the lot: three facts, none of them about your site.

    Google has been open about why. In a Q&A on Search updates, it remarked it changes Search thousands of times a year and reveals the ones it considers notable, about 10 a year when it last counted in public. Its core updates documentation adds that smaller core updates go out continually and aren’t declared at all. So a named update is a ranking change that Google decided to put on a calendar. The calendar entry tells you when. It tells you nothing about what changed, or about what happens in between.

    The announcement shrank to a timestamp, and the commentary expanded to fill the space.

    The date does have a use. Google’s own guidance uses it: wait a week after the rollout finishes, then compare that week with the week before it started. The date draws a line through your data so you know where to look. Visibility trackers do a similar job across the market; they show which sites moved.

    Recent findings suggest that what neither of them demonstrates is why. Which system changed, and why it moved your site in particular, is known inside Google and nowhere else. A rank tracker and a strong feeling won’t close that gap.

    According to recent reports, that hasn’t slowed anyone down. An obscure tool vendor published a winners-and-losers study of the November enhancement within a day or two of the launch. It gave the wrong start date and called it the sixth core update of the year. Google’s dashboard lists three. I’d say the analysis was rushed, but that implies there was something to analyze.

    The closest thing I know to a core upgrade is the annual performance review.

    Anyone who has had a job knows the meeting. You walk in and get a rating that was settled long before the meeting was booked. It reflects the year you had. It also reflects the people you were measured against, because plenty of companies calibrate ratings across a team; you can do the same work as last year and drop a grade because three colleagues did better. Search works the same way. A page is ranked against every other page that could answer the query, so a site can lose ground without changing anything.

    According to recent reports, A core update is review day. It’s when the rating becomes visible. Nobody sensible leaves that meeting and asks what changed about the meeting.

    The comparison stops in one place. After a review you get a manager, written feedback and a chance to ask what went wrong. After a core revision you get a dashboard entry. That missing conversation is the entire market for update commentary: an industry of people offering to be the manager who explains your rating, none of whom were in the calibration room.

    It has been revealed that the strongest objection to all this is that the losses are real, and it’s correct. Companies do lose a large share of their organic revenue overnight, and people lose jobs over it. The practitioners who spend their time on recoveries are dealing with real businesses in real trouble.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s also evidence that sometimes the reviewer gets it wrong. In October 2024, Google invited a group of independent publishers hit by the September 2023 helpful content revision to its campus. According to people who were in the room, they were told their content wasn’t the problem, and that they shouldn’t count on getting their traffic back. That is an awkward fact for anyone, me included, who says most affected sites had it coming.

    Look at what it does to the recovery guide, though. If the content wasn’t the issue, “seven steps for improving your content” were never going to work. The publishers with the best case against Google are also the best evidence that nobody outside it could diagnose them.

    Now the less sympathetic group, which in my experience is the bigger one.

    Most of the affected sites I’ve been asked to look at over 20 years had the same history. Somebody decided what they could get away with before finding out what the market already offered. They hadn’t researched what customers needed or looked at how good the existing answers were. They picked keywords with volume, wrote about them, and debuted.

    Sources indicate that when that didn’t work, they went looking for a shortcut, and social media had plenty. A thread with a promise that was too good to be true, and was. A “hack” from somebody who discovered SEO in the summer and by autumn had a conference slot and a YouTube channel. In office terms, that’s career advice from the colleague who joined in August and already runs a workshop. They copied it without asking why it would work. Some of these tricks do work for a few months, which is the worst outcome available, because the fall then lands inside an update window and gets blamed on the update.

    It has been revealed that then they hired SEO to make it work, as if rankings were a delivery service for businesses that forgot to have a product. I’ve written about the wall that approach runs into; it hasn’t moved.

    This is the employee who did the minimum all year and arrives at the review certain that the rating system has changed, and has brought printouts. In fairness to them, they have a problem that needs solving. “The algorithm changed” is something you can say to a board. “We built a site with nothing to say and then paid someone to get it found” tends not to make the deck.

    So there’s a buyer for an outside cause, and the enhancement coverage supplies one. It comes with a diagnosis nobody outside Google could have made and a retainer that renews before the next update can contradict it. The seller gets a client, and the client gets a story. The site stays exactly as useful as it was, which was the problem.

    This trade feels legitimate to the people in it because of how the industry thinks about quality.

    Take E-E-A-T. Google coined it for its quality raters, and Google’s own documentation says it isn’t a specific ranking factor. The industry read that and sold E-E-A-T audits anyway, with scores for a thing Google says it has no score for. Somewhere there is an author bio that was added to fix a business model.

    According to recent reports, the traits themselves are older than the initialism. Peter Morville’s user experience honeycomb had “credible,” “useful,” and “valuable” in it in 2004, as facets of a product, with no ranking attached. The industry needed Google to hand it an initialism before it noticed that people prefer things they can trust.

    “JavaScript SEO” has the same shape: it’s progressive enhancement, which web developers were practicing before anyone gave it a conference track. I made that case in Stop Learning SEO and won’t repeat it.

    If quality is a list of items to tick, then a core update is a upcoming edition of the list, and you need someone to tell you what’s on it. There is never a shortage of volunteers. Back in the office, that’s working to the KPIs. The person who works to the KPIs has to know the moment they change. The person who is good at the job mostly finds out on review day that they still are.

    So people who hold quality as a checklist need each upgrade explained; the announcement explains nothing, and so somebody makes one up.

    Recent findings suggest that the first question a business could ask after an update is “What did this update change for my site?” Answering it would take the list of systems that changed, how much each one counts, and what every competing page did in the same fortnight. Nobody outside Google has those. You can still pay for an answer. It’ll arrive as a confident PDF with a traffic-light table, and it will tell you to improve content quality, show more expertise, and prune the thin pages.

    In a recent development, now read the PDF from the update before. It notes the same thing. So will the one after the next update, because the advice was never derived from the update. If the remedy is the same whatever changed, the change taught nobody anything.

    The second question is “what do the people I want as customers need that they can’t already get?” It’s a worse question to be asked. It has no villain and no deadline; it can’t be handed to a thread, and the answer may be that the business has nothing to add yet. It’s also slower and more expensive to answer than a PDF. But it can be answered by people you can find and talk to, and it could have been answered before the site debuted.

    According to recent reports, the fair objection to the second question is Google. Google is in the business of taking in what other people know and serving it back as its own answer, and AI Overviews and AI Mode have made that the main event. The part of the web where people found you through a search result is being eaten, and Google is the one holding the fork. I’ve covered what that did to publishers’ traffic. So why polish anything for a channel that’s shrinking?

    Because the second question was never about the channel. A site is a product, and what people need from it doesn’t change when fewer of them arrive through Google. What does change is how much of what you know you should hand over for free. I’ve argued that publishing everything is a terrible business strategy, and I still think so. Holding back the method is sensible. Shipping a site that’s a bare outline of what you’re supposed to be good at is a different decision, and it fails the customer long before it fails a ranking system.

    The line between those two is thin, and it’s meant to be. It sits in a different place for every business, and no revision, checklist, or thread will tell you where yours is. A search engine certainly won’t; it looks after its own interests, as it always has. The only people who know how much is enough are the ones you’re trying to sell to, which is one more reason to go and ask them.

    In the office, it’s the gap between “what did the calibration committee change this year?” and “what did I do this year?” Only one of those is yours to find out, and it’s the one that doesn’t come with somebody else to blame.

    According to recent reports, google will post another sentence soon enough. The recovery guide for it already exists. It’s the one from last time.

    #31911. Tech Report: Google Ads Surcharges Rise To 3% In France And Italy – Local US Advertisers Can Be Billed Too via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1336 w)

    Tech Report: Google Ads Surcharges Rise To 3% In France And Italy – Local US Advertisers Can Be Billed Too via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1336 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you manage a Google Ads account, you probably got an email last week saying that ads served in France and Italy will carry a 3% Regulatory Operating Cost starting Jan.
    • I do some pro bono consulting for a retailer on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, and I have access to his Google Ads account.
    • According to recent reports, I scanned them and moved on.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you manage a Google Ads account, you probably got an email last week saying that ads served in France and Italy will carry a 3% Regulatory Operating Cost starting Jan. 1, 2027. You may have deleted it because you don’t advertise in Europe. Don’t assume you’re off the hook. Google bills these surcharges based on where your ads are actually served, and its default location setting can serve your ads to people who have never set foot in your target area.

    I found this out the practical way. I do some pro bono consulting for a retailer on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, and I have access to his Google Ads account. His campaigns are built to reach shoppers within a few miles of his store. On the morning of Nov. 11, his account received two notices from Google Payments, one headed “Surcharge Updates for Ads Served in Italy” and the other “Surcharge Updates for Ads Served in France.”.

    According to recent reports, I scanned them and moved on. Then I went back, because I suspected plenty of Search Engine Journal readers were asking the same question I was. Why is a neighborhood retailer in Newly introduced York getting billing notices about two countries he isn’t targeting?

    The short answer is that the emails are a warning, not a bill. Whether they become a bill depends on settings most local advertisers have never opened.

    Google calls these charges jurisdiction-specific surcharges. Some are labeled Digital Services Tax (DST) fees and some are labeled Regulatory Operating Costs, but they work the same way. They are added to your invoice on top of your ad spend, and on top of any account budget you set.

    It has been revealed that here is how the rates for Google Ads stand on Google’s help page, before and after Jan. 1, 2027.

    Two former entries are off the list. Google says ads served in India stopped carrying a 2% charge on Sept. 1, 2024, and ads served in Canada no longer carry the 2.5% DST fee.

    The same increases apply to Display & Video 360, and Google’s help page indicates YouTube placements bought on a reservation basis carry the surcharges too.

    In Italy, the jump is half a point. In France, it is a full point, which means the fee itself rises by 50%. Turkey moves the other way.

    See also: Ask A PPC: How Will The Tariffs Impact My PPC Campaigns?

    Google’s help page states the rule plainly. The charge applies every time an ad is served in one of these jurisdictions, “regardless of where your actual business is located.” The surcharge is calculated on the impressions or clicks served in each country, so an account that serves nothing in France pays nothing in France.

    In a recent development, that would seem to settle it for my client. But a few paragraphs further down, Google adds a warning that you might show ads to users in a country you never targeted “because your business is in a location of interest for them.” Google also notes it is the advertiser’s responsibility to make sure campaign target settings are correct, and that it will not refund surcharges triggered by legitimate clicks and impressions served according to those settings.

    In plain English, if your settings let a shopper in Milan see your ad, you pay the Italy surcharge on that impression, and you don’t get it back.

    See also: 13 Google Ads Settings To Check When Running International PPC Campaigns.

    Recent findings suggest that google’s advanced location options give you two choices for who counts as being in your target area. “Presence or interest” reaches people who are in, regularly in, or who’ve shown interest in your targeted locations. “Presence” reaches only people who are in or regularly in them.

    Sources indicate that presence or interest is the default, and Google labels it as recommended. Google supports that recommendation with its own data, saying advertisers in travel, real estate, and education who switched to it saw 5% more conversions on Search campaigns. That is Google’s claim from Google’s internal data, and it covers three verticals, not retail.

    For a store on Madison Avenue, “interest” is where Europe gets in. Someone in Paris searching for shops on the Upper East Side has shown interest in Fresh York. Under the default, your ad can serve to that person, and the impression lands in France.

    The controls have also been widening. Demand Gen campaigns picked up the same Presence or interest versus Presence choice in late 2025, and AI Max for Search has added options for reaching people based on locations of interest. More automation in where ads go means more chances to serve impressions in places you didn’t pick.

    Giovanni Perilli, a funnel marketing consultant who writes about European ad costs, published a breakdown the same day the emails went out. The France email he received did not mention Italy at all. In his words, the email “leaves out the change that matters most to anyone advertising in Italy.”.

    Recent findings suggest that that matches my own experience, with a twist. My client’s account got two separate emails, one per country. Advertisers who received only one should check the help page rather than assume nothing else changed.

    Perilli also turns the surcharge into numbers a PPC manager can use. Because the fee is added on top of what you spend, he multiplies a cost-per-acquisition by 1.03 and divides a return on ad spend by 1.03. A €40 CPA effectively becomes €41.20. A ROAS of four becomes about 3.88. If your break-even ROAS is 2.5, your real target in France and Italy is now about 2.58.

    According to recent reports, those are small numbers. On thin retail margins in the first quarter, they are not nothing.

    See also: Google Notes Changing tCPA & Budgets Won’t Reset Learning – 6 BFCM Takeaways.

    According to recent reports, google’s help page says the France and Italy charges cover part of the cost of complying with digital services tax legislation in those countries. The tax news over the past year lines up with that.

    It has been revealed that french lawmakers voted in October 2025 to double France’s digital services tax from 3% to 6% for the largest platforms, but the budget bill carrying it was rejected a month later, and the rate remains 3%. Italy’s DST has applied at a 3% rate since 2020, and its 2025 budget law removed the domestic revenue threshold that had kept some companies out of scope. Turkey went the other direction, cutting its DST from 7.5% to 5% this year and to 2.5% on Jan. 1, 2027. Google’s Turkey surcharge falls to 2.25% on the same date.

    Google also has company now. Meta began charging its own location fees on July 1, 2026, at 3% in France, Italy, and Spain, as Bloomberg reported. From January, Google and Meta charge the same 3% in all three countries.

    Sources indicate that here’s my read. Digital services taxes were sold to voters as a way to make significant tech pay. The platforms are now itemizing those taxes on advertisers’ invoices, and some of those advertisers are small businesses on another continent. Whatever you think of the policy, the bill has moved down the chain, and PPC managers are the ones who have to explain it to clients.

    Here are four steps I’m taking in my client’s account, and I’d suggest you take them in yours.

    I almost ignored these notices, and I’ve been reading Google Ads billing emails since 2003. My advice is to treat them as an audit prompt, not as spam. The surcharge itself is modest. The real story is how many local accounts may be serving ads in Europe without anyone deciding they should.

    My client’s ads are meant for the Upper East Side, not Paris or Milan. I’d rather confirm that in a report before Jan. 1 than discover it on a February invoice.

    Senior Manager, Business Operations at Clutch

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1321 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, clutch is at a pivotal moment.
    • According to recent reports, this is a people manager role.
    • When something important doesn't have an owner yet, it lands with you: a partnership strategy, a latest commercial model, or pricing and margin guidance for leadership.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, clutch is at a pivotal moment. We're growing significantly year over year, and we need more connective tissue to keep pace. We're hiring a Senior Manager, Business Operations to connect the commercial side of the house, so the teams that win, onboard, and retain our customers work from the same facts and toward the same goals. This role sits in Finance.

    According to recent reports, this is a people manager role. You'll lead our Revenue Operations (RevOps) team and act as an operating partner to senior leaders across Sales, Marketing, Customer Success, Implementation, People, and Finance. Together with the RevOps team, you own the shared language of the business (definitions, data, and processes) so commercial teams make decisions from one view of it.

    When something important doesn't have an owner yet, it lands with you: a partnership strategy, a latest commercial model, or pricing and margin guidance for leadership. This is a fast-moving startup. We're building toward a much larger firm but we aren't one yet, and most of this role has no playbook. You'll define the process, build the tool, and hand it to the team. If you want established structure, this likely isn't the role.

    You'll report to the Director of Business Operations and work directly with senior leaders across the manufacturer as a neutral partner to every function rather than an advocate for one. Your work will be visible, and it will significantly influence how we make commercial decisions.

    According to recent reports, you'll lead a small, high-ownership RevOps team that runs the systems and data our commercial teams depend on, and creates leverage for them to do their jobs even better. The team doesn't just own systems. They build automation, tooling, and processes, and they're close partners to Sales and Marketing. You'll coach them, set priorities, and open up more strategic scope, while giving them real autonomy.

    Learn the business end to end: the revenue funnel, the customer lifecycle, how each commercial team works day to day, and where decisions get stuck.

    Build trust with your RevOps team: learn the work they own, and set priorities and team rhythms together.

    Deliver the first version of client-level margin and cost-to-serve, the analysis that grounds our pricing strategy.

    Develop a first point of view on pricing and packaging for revenue leadership, built on that analysis.

    Put AI to work in your own workflow from week one, and identify the first set of manual, repetitive processes across the commercial teams worth automating.

    Stand up a first version of a deal desk, including an approval workflow, pricing and discount guardrails, and standard commercial terms.

    Partner with Sales and Marketing leaders as they prepare for the monthly business review: pressure-test their prepares and point out risks, then solve them with the RevOps team by creating upcoming processes, tooling, or automation.

    Build on the strength of the RevOps team: prioritize its roadmap against business outcomes and take on more strategic work together.

    Launch your first AI-enabled workflows or automations that remove manual reporting or reconciliation for the commercial teams, with time saved tracked.

    Have a team whose output and standards hold, with the processes, tooling, and automation you've built running without you in the room.

    Have AI-enabled, self-serve tooling that commercial teams use day to day, with measurable time savings.

    Be the person leadership trusts to pick up the next notable thing that doesn't have an owner yet.

    5-8 years of total experience that combines consulting or banking with time as an operator inside a tech giant.

    Experience managing people: you've coached ICs, given direct feedback, made tough talent calls, and built team rhythms.

    Startup experience. You've worked in a fast-moving, ever-changing environment where structure wasn't already there, and you built it. This is not a role for someone whose experience is only at large, established enterprises.

    Strong analytical and financial modeling skills, including forecasting. You're very comfortable building models in spreadsheets from scratch, and they hold up to scrutiny. You use AI to move faster and sharpen your work, and you have the foundational modeling knowledge to know when its output is wrong.

    Data-first and self-sufficient. You open the dataset before you build the slide, you're always looking for more data to test an idea, and you're comfortable getting into raw data yourself. You use AI to analyze it faster and know enough to check its work.

    Commercial acumen: you can read commercial terms, spot the problematic ones, and reason about pricing, discounting, margin, and deal structure.

    A clear communicator who can walk an executive through a messy problem and leave them with a decision, and who is just as effective working alongside an AE, a CSM, or an engineer.

    #31909. 6.9% Of ChatGPT Conversations Demonstrated Purchase Intent In U.S. Panel via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1178 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    6.9% Of ChatGPT Conversations Demonstrated Purchase Intent In U.S. Panel via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1178 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Brands have some insight into how often purchase intent shows up in chat with ChatGPT, based on its presence in 6.9% of conversations in a U.S.
    • Data was provided by Verso, which tracks people’ ChatGPT conversation history when they link their account.
    • Of ChatGPT’s responses in this sub-sample, 87.9% did not name a single brand, product or business.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Brands have some insight into how often purchase intent shows up in chat with ChatGPT, based on its presence in 6.9% of conversations in a U.S. opt-in panel analyzed by SparkToro.

    Data was provided by Verso, which tracks people’ ChatGPT conversation history when they link their account. The sample size is 41,961 conversations, generated by 12,321 people between Jan. 1 and Oct. 29, 2026. Most of the figures are from a sub-sample which had been statistically weighted to match the demographic characteristics of the U.S. population.

    Of ChatGPT’s responses in this sub-sample, 87.9% did not name a single brand, product or business. Based on the analysis, Rand Fishkin (co-founder and CEO of SparkToro) concluded that the primary reason AI visibility matters is Google’s implementation of AI Overviews and AI Mode, rather than ChatGPT itself.

    It has been revealed that based upon the purchase-intent graph developed with the weighted group, there are three types of conversation by purpose. In a total of 4.9% of conversations, the person planned to purchase and was continuing to look at the options; another 2.1% were asking questions related to purchasing a specific brand, product or service; while a total of 93.1% showed no intention to purchase.

    Fishkin wrote, “I suspect this is bad news for ChatGPT’s advertising opportunities.”.

    Sources indicate that he also referenced SparkToro’s December 2024 analysis of approximately 332 million Google searches. He wrote that 15% or more of searches fit his definition. SparkToro did an analysis of searches done by a U.S. panel via browsers from January 2023 through September 2024. Commercial (a financial, business services or commerce intent) accounted for 14.5% of searches, although the searcher may not have been ready to make a purchase at that time.

    Sources indicate that transactional accounted for 0.69%. These categories do not match the categories identified in the ChatGPT graph which measured purchase intentions, so the percentages cannot be compared directly.

    According to recent reports, in addition to tracking whether people asked about brands, the report also tracked if ChatGPT’s responses named any. In the weighted group, 86.7% of all prompts did not ask for brand, product or company information. Of all prompts, 6.6% asked about several brands, with the remainder being about a single brand (6.7%). On the response side, 7.0% of all responses mentioned multiple brands, products or companies while 5.1% mentioned one; the post’s reported percentage of responses mentioning at least one was 12.1%.

    The post’s takeaways describe 12% of ChatGPT usage as part of the buyer journey, though its purchase-intent chart puts conversations with purchase intent at 6.9%.

    Recent findings suggest that images and visual design requests were the top ranked category in the report with a total of 17.6% of conversations. Information and entertainment came second in terms of overall conversations (14.4%), writing and communication third (12.7%), while shopping, brands and local services made up 5.3%.

    Sources indicate that one category per conversation was assigned, representing the primary goal of each. The output type counts over the topic when someone asks ChatGPT to create something (e.g., if you ask it to write an email asking for a refund from PayPal, that would be categorized as writing instead of shopping).

    Sources indicate that the percentages shown in the report’s chart vary from the percentages shown in the report’s text by less than two percentage points per category. The percentages provided here reflect the report’s chart.

    Industry observers note that the panel was also compared to OpenAI’s Signals data for September using the weighted group. OpenAI’s data was heavier towards writing and tech support, while the weighted panel data leaned more toward image requests and how-to questions. The author claims the two are fair to compare given that OpenAI almost certainly includes API requests (that Verso does not track) in its numbers.

    According to OpenAI’s page, the dataset “reflects only messages within ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, and Pro accounts” and Codex and enterprise usage are excluded from this count; thus excluding API calls as well. In addition, OpenAI presents global message shares whereas the panel indicates shares of U.S.-based conversations.

    It has been revealed that verso offers a free tool that breaks down a person’s ChatGPT history. Its sign-up terms say Verso stores the imported conversations and includes them, de-identified, in datasets it licenses to research and business customers. According to the post, Verso co-founder Aaron Aknin reached out to the post’s author and supplied the data.

    The report also described the panel as skewed toward younger people, women and people at lower income levels. There were 9,675 members in the panel that had demographic information that could be used as a weighting base to match the 2024 United States Census. No usage category varied by more than 1.4 percentage points when the demographics were weighted to these standards.

    Industry observers note that before the data analysis was performed, the 131 heaviest consumers, who generated an average of over 33 prompts per active month, were eliminated. These heavy users accounted for approximately 1% of the total number of panelists, but they were responsible for sending 21% of all prompts. On average each member of the weighted group (excluding the above noted heaviest users) sent 9.9 prompts between January and October.

    According to recent reports, as most panelists were recorded on mobile phones, the post indicates this may have caused some of the usage through desktop computers and work accounts to be underreported. API requests are not included in the data set.

    In a recent development, each conversation was coded using a written code book provided to Anthropic’s model called Claude. Each conversation was coded based upon its title, up to six of the user-generated prompts, the initial few lines of ChatGPT’s first few responses and any product cards or bolded names. A second coder independently recoded a random sample of conversations, and the two coders agreed on categories 90% of the time and on brand tags 97% to 99% of the time. The post reports no separate agreement figure regarding its identification of purchase intent.

    SparkToro sells audience research software.

    For brands splitting AI visibility and ad budgets, the U.S. panel gives a measured share of ChatGPT conversations that involve buying, and it’s under 7%. Fishkin concludes that Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode are what make AI visibility vital, and he questions whether tracking ChatGPT visibility is worth it unless Bing rankings and AI visibility are tracked too.

    The post explains that the panel reflects what people ask ChatGPT much better than how often they use it. For PPC teams exploring ChatGPT Ads, the 6.9% purchase-intent share offers a snapshot of the conversation mix in a consumer panel with light ChatGPT use, not a count of purchase-related conversations across ChatGPT.

    According to recent reports, until panel data includes desktop, work and API use, it’s best to pair purchase-intent figures like this one with your own ChatGPT referral and ad data before adding them to a budget strategy. Fishkin also shared that he looks forward to doing more research with Verso.

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1126 w)
    📖 Baca

    Industry News: Google Explains How To Avoid CDN Migration SEO Problems via @sejournal, @martinibuster

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that googlers Gary Illyes and Cherry Prommawin explain how moving to a CDN can unexpectedly increase crawling and overwhelm the origin server, despite eventually improving website performance.
    • Illyes and Prommawin explained that moving to a CDN can cause Googlebot to increase crawling because faster server responses signal that the site’s infrastructure can handle more requests.
    • CDN caches are initially empty and the CDN only starts caching when a browser or bot requests a page at which point the request has to be forwarded to the origin server, where the actual website is at.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that googlers Gary Illyes and Cherry Prommawin explain how moving to a CDN can unexpectedly increase crawling and overwhelm the origin server, despite eventually improving website performance. They also share that attempts to control crawler traffic can sometimes accidentally block Googlebot and harm Search visibility.

    Illyes and Prommawin explained that moving to a CDN can cause Googlebot to increase crawling because faster server responses signal that the site’s infrastructure can handle more requests. Google’s automated crawling systems interpret the improved performance as an indication that more crawling is possible and responds by gradually increasing the crawl rate.

    CDN caches are initially empty and the CDN only starts caching when a browser or bot requests a page at which point the request has to be forwarded to the origin server, where the actual website is at.

    When Google increases the crawl rate, the initial crawl is handled by the origin server. But now Googlebot is hitting the server more aggressively and it’s this that can overwhelm the origin server, initially.

    “For one, suddenly the crawling metrics suggests the site can handle a larger amount of crawling. And on the flip side, because the CDN caches aren’t yet populated, the origin server still has to serve the requested pages.

    Basically, CDNs take the valve off the hose, so now crawlers are drinking from a fire hose.”.

    Cherry Prommawin added more details:.

    Sources indicate that “Under normal circumstances, our crawlers operate under an key rule. When a server responds faster, the crawlers assume the infrastructure is healthy and slowly ramp up crawl speed.

    …So the crawlers see how fast the server responds, get really excited, and start to crawl the entire site at a higher, higher, and higher speed. But it’s a trap.

    People assume a CDN can catch a crawl spike from day one, but …The cache has to be filled up with the assets off the site first.”.

    Gary Illyes explained that on a first request for a page the CDN has to fetch the page from the origin server first to populate the cache with the content. It’s not until the second request for the page that the cache is populated with the content and begins doing its job.

    According to recent reports, “…which means your origin server may get slammed by the flood anyway. Now, to be fair, our crawlers take time to ramp up. It won’t happen in a millisecond.

    An empty cache means your origin server is still doing all the heavy lifting. Until that cache is populated, your CDN isn’t acting as a shield just yet.”.

    In a recent development, A CDN cannot serve an un-cached URL without retrieving it first from the origin server and that only happens after a request for that URL is first made. Crawlers visit large numbers of URLs virtually all the time and can generate a substantial amount of origin traffic before the CDN’s caches are fully populated.

    According to recent reports, this next concern involves accidentally blocking Googlebot and triggering a reduced search presence because Google can no longer crawl and index URLs from a website. Illyes and Prommawin explain it in the context of a website admin flipping a switch at Cloudflare and inadvertently blocking Googlebot.

    This is a real problem, I recall an instance in which a popular website’s massive traffic dried up whenever Cloudflare was activated and would return once they turned it off. They had a devil of a time diagnosing why this was happening and the customer service people at the time were unable to help them. It may have been the case, as Illyes and Prommawin noted, that the admin had turned on a strict bot filter that inadvertently blocked Googlebot.

    Illyes offered an example of an admin doing exactly that:.

    “They look at the spiking traffic, assume they are being aggressively scraped by botnets, and naturally, they panic.”.

    And what sometimes happens next is that an admin might turn on “blanket security rules” that block Googlebot.

    Prommawin offered more details:.

    …If the CDN detects automated requests, it intercepts them with a CAPTCHA challenge, asking them to click pictures of traffic lights to prove they’re human.

    …It sees automated requests, flags it as a bot, and then intercepts with a CAPTCHA. And since our crawlers cannot identify a traffic light, they fail the test.”.

    What eventually happens with prolonged Googlebot blocking is that Google will begin dropping the pages from the index.

    Prommawin suggested that site admins should configure their CDN to allow known and trusted crawlers. This is a method called whitelisting where only crawlers that are on the “allowed” list can get it and all other crawlers cannot.

    They also recommend the use of CDN-level rate limiting of Googlebot if the requests on the origin server lead to downtime which can negatively impact legitimate human traffic to the website.

    Sources indicate that when a site initially starts out with a CDN, the CDN does not have a cache of a website’s content. The cache doesn’t get loaded until it’s requested by a browser or crawler visit.

    In a recent development, cache pre-warming is the process of requesting content from a site so that the content gets loaded onto the CDN. This ensures that the content is already loaded onto the CDN before users request it, which ensures that the content is delivered swiftly without the CDN having to first retrieve it from the origin server (the server where the actual content files exist).

    Illyes recommends “pre-warming” the cache by programmatically requesting URLs from it so that thE cache is populated in a controlled manner.

    “And to survive augmenting your site with a CDN, see if you can pre-warm the caches by programmatically fetching your top URLs through the CDN before you open the floodgates to search engines.”.

    Sources indicate that google’s main point is that moving to a CDN can create an unexpected combination of faster crawling and increased origin-server demand. That in turn can lead to unintentionally setting aggressive security restrictions that prevent Googlebot from accessing a website.

    Three especially important points for SEOs and site owners:.

    Recent findings suggest that 1. Using a CDN can trigger an increase in Googlebot crawling when it detects faster server responses, even though the CDN’s caches have not yet been populated, which in turn means an increase in requests for URLs from the origin server.

    2. A CDN migration can inadvertently cause pages to disappear from Google Search due to aggressive security settings intended to stop malicious bots can also lock out Google’s crawlers.

    In a recent development, 3. Google recommends pre-warming caches, allowing trusted crawlers, and temporarily controlling crawling when server demand becomes excessive.

    Read Google’s latest CDN documentation here.
